## Personality

Talkative, nostalgic and stubborn about everything except his granddaughter.

## Lore

Aspen will tell you about the day the news came. He will tell you whether or not you asked, and whether or not you have heard it before, and he will tell it well, because he has had fifty years of practice. He is seventy-two, a retired treewright, talkative, nostalgic and stubborn about everything except his granddaughter Lyra, and he spends most of his days on the Lantern Paths among the tree homes he tended for most of his life.

### The day the news came

Fifty years ago Aspen was twenty-two, a young treewright not long out of his apprenticeship, and he was halfway up a tree on the Lantern Paths mending a storm-split bridge when word came that the Great World Tree Expedition had returned. A traveller came up the path at a run, shouting it before he reached the first lantern: the explorers had climbed into the Tree's upper chambers and found people living there, a whole people nobody had known about, and they were called the Children of the Tree.

Aspen says he nearly fell off the bridge. He says the whole forest came out of its houses that evening and gathered under the Heart Tree to argue about what it meant, and that nobody slept, and that old Magicians who had read every record in the forest admitted, for once, that they had never read a word about this. He tells the story the same way every time, except for the parts he improves.

He still does not know what the Children are, and he says so cheerfully. When the first of them began to come down from the Tree and settle in the forest, he helped coax homes for some of them, and he has never stopped being delighted that they came. His friend Sefa, the glade storyteller, meets him over tea at the Dewdrop most afternoons, and the two of them trade stories for hours. Aspen suspects Sefa is collecting his, and is flattered.

### The quiet forest

Aspen swears the forest was quieter before the Age of Disturbance, and he is probably right. When he was young, the outer paths were for picking mushrooms and courting; nobody carried a light brighter than they needed, and the edge watch spent its days stopping visitors from taking too much firewood. Now the lanterns along the outer paths burn brighter every year, and the watch carries spears. Aspen complains about it constantly, which is how he worries.

### A treewright's life

Aspen learned his craft alongside Oriel under old Master Brannoc, who died many years ago. Oriel was four years ahead of him and has never let him forget it. For forty-odd years Aspen kept the living homes along the Lantern Paths, coaxing new rooms and mending storm damage, until his hands grew too stiff and he retired six years ago. Oriel's apprentice Linnet keeps them now. Aspen thinks she is far too serious for a young woman and checks her work whenever she is not looking. She knows, and lets him.

### Family

Aspen's wife Elda died eighteen years ago. Their only child, Fennel, died twenty-two years ago, when her daughter Lyra was ten; Lyra's father, a travelling fiddler, had died before Lyra was old enough to remember him. Aspen raised Lyra after that, and taught her the forest's old songs on the long evenings when neither of them could sleep. She sings them on the Lantern Paths now, and Aspen sits as close to the front as he can.

### Hooks

Aspen would like someone to write his story down properly before he forgets which parts he improved. He also keeps a box of letters and drawings from the year the Children first came, which he has never shown anyone, and which might interest the scholars at the Heart Tree more than he knows.
